name: Accessible first
summary: Large text, large targets and AAA contrast, so everyone can finish the task.
description: Accessible first is an Open DS scheme: a full set of answers to the Open DS grammar, with the reasons behind each, usage rules, voice and tone, and the tokens that follow. Large text, large targets and AAA contrast, so everyone can finish the task.

ai.use_when: Public services, health, government and any product that must work for everyone.
ai.avoid_when: Dense expert tools where screen space matters more than size.

People must finish the form, and a carousel suits content where missing some is fine. Content people must see does not belong in slides.
Command is for expert users who jump anywhere by typing. Here people do this once or twice a year and nobody remembers the interface.
Context menus are for power users. Here nobody remembers the interface, and every action looks like a button people can find.
Data table is for finding and acting on many records, often in bulk. Accessible first avoids dense expert tools, and its one density has no compact mode.
Only dialogs separate from the page here, with a dimmed page and a border. A sliding panel adds a second layer the scheme does not use.
Every action here looks like a button people can find. Row actions are a secondary button with a word, not a menu.
Touch screens have no hover, and public services are used on any device. A person with a tremor completes a form on a tablet.
Kbd tells people the shortcut for an action. Here people do this once or twice a year, and nobody remembers the interface from last time.
Menubar is for dense desktop-style tools. Accessible first avoids dense expert tools, and nobody remembers the interface from last time.
Optional help here sits in a section a person can open, in the page. One clear way to do each thing leaves no room for a floating panel too.
Resizing means dragging panels in desktop tools. The scheme avoids widgets that need drag or precise pointing, and avoids dense expert tools.
A component joins only when it works with any assistive technology. The native select covers the same choice and every assistive technology understands it.
Only dialogs separate from the page here, with a dimmed page and a border. A panel sliding in from an edge adds a layer the scheme does not use.
Sidebar is for apps people move around all session. Here people do this once or twice a year, and breadcrumb shows where they are.
Spinner already says the page is working. Accessible first keeps one clear way to do each thing, so a second loading state is not added.
The scheme avoids widgets that need drag or precise pointing. A person with a tremor completes a form here, and an exact answer is typed.
Components do their work in forms and steps, where a choice waits for the form. The catalogue gives that case to the checkbox.
A toast goes away. Here errors and important notes stay on the page, because people must know what went wrong and where.
Icons never stand alone here, so no control needs a hover hint. Touch screens never hover, and optional help sits in a section a person can open.

open-ds.why: radius.6: Buttons and inputs take the 6px corner: slightly rounded, never a pill, so they still read as clear fields and buttons.
radius.4: Badges and checkboxes take the smallest corner, 4px, so a status keeps a clear rectangle around its word, never a pill.
radius.4: the panel's 8px corner less its 4px padding, so an option's corner nests inside the menu's.
radius.6: the control corner; it is not a pill, so a growing box keeps it.
radius.8: Cards, menus and dialogs take the largest corner, 8px, so a container's corner differs from the 6px controls inside it.

open-ds.why: Big, even steps give an 8px base. Spacious density starts the tight gap at one and a half steps, so even close parts stay apart at high zoom.

We use 12px for the tight gap between the parts of one item in order to group and separate: one and a half base steps (1.5 × 8px), the smallest gap. Distance does this by grouping what is near and separating what is far, as the eye reads proximity (Gestalt), so a gap between groups stays clearly larger than a gap inside one. So parts read as one item and stay apart at high zoom, because steps are big and even (spacing.definition) and everyone uses it, including people with disabilities (people.q1).

We use 16px for the default gap between the items of one group, such as fields, in order to group and separate: two base steps (2 × 8px), 4px more than the tight gap. Distance does this by grouping what is near and separating what is far, as the eye reads proximity (Gestalt), so a gap between groups stays clearly larger than a gap inside one. So people with tremor tap the field they mean, because the layout is spacious (spacing.values) and space between fields matters most (spacing.lands).

We use 32px for the group gap between groups of questions in order to group and separate: four base steps (4 × 8px), twice the default gap. Distance does this by grouping what is near and separating what is far, as the eye reads proximity (Gestalt), so a gap between groups stays clearly larger than a gap inside one. So people see where one group of questions ends and the next begins, because the layout is spacious (spacing.values) and each step must take low effort to understand (human.q1).

We use 48px for the section gap between page sections in order to group and separate: six base steps (6 × 8px), half again the group gap. Distance does this by grouping what is near and separating what is far, as the eye reads proximity (Gestalt), so a gap between groups stays clearly larger than a gap inside one. So sections part by space, which is easy to see, and not by thin lines, because the layout is spacious (spacing.values) and steps are big and even (spacing.definition).

We use 24px for the inline padding inside controls in order to give content room inside its box: three base steps (3 × 8px), the same as a card's padding. Padding does this by keeping content off the edge of its box, so the content reads as part of that box, and by setting the size of the box with the content. So each button is a bigger target that is easy to hit, because everyone uses it, including people with motor needs (people.q1), and the smallest target is large (accessibility.values).

We use 24px for the padding inside cards and dialogs in order to give content room inside its box: three base steps (3 × 8px), half again the default gap. Padding does this by keeping content off the edge of its box, so the content reads as part of that box, and by setting the size of the box with the content. So content stays clear of the strong border at any zoom, because everyone uses it (people.q1) and each step must take low effort to understand (human.q1).

We use 16px for the inline padding inside table cells in order to give content room inside its box: two base steps (2 × 8px), the same as the default gap. Padding does this by keeping content off the edge of its box, so the content reads as part of that box, and by setting the size of the box with the content. So values in two columns stay apart at high zoom, because everyone uses it, including people with low vision (people.q1), and the layout is spacious (spacing.values).

A large target sets the 52px default. The step is 4px, so compact stays at the 48px large target size; large equals the default, as every control is already large. Rows are a decision of their own, one step taller than a control.

default.$description: Height of buttons and inputs, and the smallest target.

open-ds.why: We use 52px for buttons and inputs in order to make a hit target: the large target size, step 0 of the control scale, a 52px hit area above the 44px of WCAG 2.5.5. Height does this by setting the hit area a finger or a pointer must hit; WCAG measures the hit area, not the drawn box (2.5.8: 24px at AA; 2.5.5: 44px at AAA), and padding or a label can make it larger than the box. So people with tremor and low vision get a large control, because the smallest target is large (accessibility.values) and everyone uses it, including people with motor needs (people.q1).

We use 48px for compact controls, such as a button inside a field, in order to make a hit target: one 4px step below the 52px default on the control scale, a short step so the 48px hit area still meets the large target size. Height does this by setting the hit area a finger or a pointer must hit; WCAG measures the hit area, not the drawn box (2.5.8: 24px at AA; 2.5.5: 44px at AAA), and padding or a label can make it larger than the box. So a button fits inside a field and is still large, because the smallest target is large (accessibility.values) and everyone uses it (people.q1).

large.$description: Height of large controls. Not used in this system, so it equals the default.

open-ds.why: We use 52px for large controls in order to make a hit target: the default's step on the control scale and the default's 52px hit area, as every control is already large and the scheme has no hero action. Height does this by setting the hit area a finger or a pointer must hit; WCAG measures the hit area, not the drawn box (2.5.8: 24px at AA; 2.5.5: 44px at AAA), and padding or a label can make it larger than the box. So every button has one height and pages stay predictable, because each step must take low effort to understand (human.q1) and the smallest target is large (accessibility.values).

We use 56px for one table row in order to keep the eye on its row: a row one 52px default control tall plus 4px, one step up the control scale, as rows are a decision of their own here. Row height does this by making each row a band the eye follows across, and a hit target when the row is clickable (WCAG 2.5.8: 24px). So rows are easy to read and tap, a little taller than the control they hold, because row heights are a spacing role, for touch and zoom (spacing.roles), and the smallest target is large (accessibility.values).

open-ds.why: Few sizes: a large 19px body and a 1.22 ratio, each role on the next step, and no step under 16px. Headings sit tight at 1.25; every other role wraps at 1.6, labels too, because a label wraps when people zoom.
Display is 35px, three ratio steps above the 19px body (19 × 1.22^3), kept off page titles: it changes from page to page and pushes the content down.
Display lines are 1.25 times its 35px size, about 44px; as a ratio, the line height grows with the text when people zoom.
Display is bold, 700, one of the two weights the scheme loads; bold and the 35px size together mark the top of the page.
Title is 28px, two ratio steps above body and one clear step under display, the same on every page, so people always know where they are.
Title lines are 1.25 times its 28px size, 35px, the same tight ratio as display, and they grow with the text on zoom.
Title is bold, 700, so the 28px page title reads as a heading and never as large body text.
Heading is 23px, one ratio step above the 19px body and one under the 28px title, so a section inside a form step stands out.
Heading lines are 1.25 times its 23px size, about 29px: the smallest role on the tight ratio, while text from 19px down takes 1.6.
Heading is bold, 700: at 23px it sits only one ratio step above body, so weight, not size alone, sets it apart.
Body is 19px, step 0 of the scale and one ratio step above the 16px caption, because large text is readable for more people.
Body lines are 1.6 times its 19px size, 30.4px: the open ratio for paragraphs, so short lines of large text lower effort.
Body is regular, 400, the plain weight for paragraphs; bold stays for the roles that mark structure.
Label shares step 0 with body at 19px, because form labels and hints are where type matters most; weight, not size, sets it apart.
Label lines are 1.6 times its 19px size, 30.4px, so a label that wraps above its field keeps the open spacing of body.
Label is bold, 700: at 19px it shares the body size, so bold marks it as the field's always visible label.
Caption is one ratio step under body (19 ÷ 1.22), 16px, exactly 1rem: even secondary text never drops below the reader's own default size.
Caption lines are 1.6 times its 16px size, 25.6px: the smallest text keeps the open ratio and grows with the text on zoom.
Caption is regular, 400, not bold: it carries secondary text, and the scheme loads only regular and bold.
Data shares step 0 with body at 19px, not a small or mono size, because every number must be readable at large size.
Data lines match body, 1.6 times 19px, 30.4px, so numbers in a table read with the same room as text.
Data is regular, 400, like body, so numbers in a table read as plain content and not as labels.
